..
Issued at 336 PM CDT Fri Aug 7 2026


General Overview...

Broad ridging out west with troughing to the east leaves the area 
underneath northwest flow today. Across the next few days, the upper-
level pattern will be expected to return back to a more zonal (less 
amplified) flow with occasional shortwave disturbance possible to 
pass through over the next week. Though a few scattered storms may 
pop up here and there over the weekend into early next week, the 
majority of the area should remain fairly dry with gradually 
increasing rain/storm chances across the middle to end of next week. 
As for temperatures, highs will gradually increase by a few degrees 
each day through Sunday before trending the other direction for a 
majority of next week. 


Tonight and Saturday...

Though some areas of fog can't be completely ruled out across a few 
locations mainly south if I-80 tonight (20-50% chance), the coverage 
and intensity of any frog that develops should not be as 
widespread/intense as this past morning. The latest HREF guidance 
has 50% of its ensemble members projecting fog with only 20% of its 
members showing dense fog. In comparison of the HREF guidance 24-
hours earlier (guidance for this past morning), 60% of its members 
had fog with 40% of them dense. As result to the decreased model 
confidence, we suspect that any fog that does manage to develop 
will not be as dense or widespread as from this past morning.

The even bigger question for Saturday morning will be the potential 
for a few storms to materialize out of the Nebraska sandhills region. 
Current high resolution forecast guidance has been in and out with the 
overall coverage of these storms, leading to lower than normal 
confidence for our PoPs (only up to 10-30%). The best chances for 
thunderstorm activity will generally be concentrated north of I-80 
and east of HWY-281 between 7AM and 2PM. 

Despite the uncertainty for storm coverage, the conditions would 
generally be supportive enough for severe weather for any given 
location that does see a thunderstorm. As a result, the SPC keeps a 
majority of the area (all of south central Nebraska and Philips, 
Smith and Jewell counties in north central Kansas) included in a 
Marginal severe weather outlook. Conditionally, some elevated CAPE 
(up to 3,000-4,000J/kg above 800mb) paired with a nocturnal low-
level jet (25-40kts of bulk shear) should be supportive enough for 
helping a few of these storms become potentially strong to severe. 
Though hail up to the size of quarters may be possible within a few 
of the taler (generally stronger) storms, the main concern would be 
for gusty thunderstorm winds up to near 60MPH. 

Beyond the chance for storms in the morning, a few isolated to 
scattered pop up storms can't be ruled out across the evening or
nighttime hours as well. Highs for Saturday are expected to 
climb back to as high as the upper 80s and 90s for a majority of
the area, though a few far southeast Nebraska and north central
Kansas locations may reach the low 100s (20-50% chances). This 
warm up will carry on through the weekend as southerly winds 
help advect in a warmer and humid airmass. 


Next Week...

Highs peaking Sunday (90-104 degrees; warmest towards the southwest) 
will be followed a multi-day cool down following the passage of a 
cold front Sunday night into Monday morning as well as the presence 
of increasing cloud coverage. NBM probabilities even show a 60-80% 
chance for highs to stay below 80 degrees Thursday for south central 
Nebraska and a 40-60% chance across north central Kansas. Though a 
heat advisory has not yet been considered for Sunday, heat indices 
will be expected to rise above 100 degrees across a majority of the 
area with a 30-70% of heat index values reaching/exceeding 105 
degrees across portions of north central Kansas. If this trend 
continues, a heat advisory may be considered. 

Besides the temperatures, a slightly wetter signal is beginning to 
appear next week as daily PoPs return across the entire area starting 
Monday night (20-30% chance). It is too early to fully analyze the 
nightly thunderstorm potential that will be mainly based around the 
specific timing for passing disturbances. That being said, sufficient 
moisture, a warm/buoyant airmass and the return of a nocturnal low-
level jet, would all check the boxes needed for severe convection.
